CHAPTER 7 - PROPERTIES OF FLUIDS

Introduction

A fluid is any substance that flows and takes the shape of its container - this includes both liquids and gases. Unlike a rigid solid, a fluid cannot sustain a shearing (tangential) force while at rest; it simply flows. In this chapter we study how fluids at rest exert pressure (hydrostatics), how they support floating and immersed bodies (buoyancy), and two surface/transport properties that shape everyday behaviour - surface tension and viscosity. Finally we study fluids in motion (hydrodynamics) through the equation of continuity and Bernoulli's theorem. These ideas explain a huge range of phenomena: why a dam is thicker at its base, how a hydraulic brake multiplies force, why a needle floats on water, why rain drops fall at a steady speed, and how an aeroplane wing generates lift.

7.1 THRUST AND PRESSURE

The total normal force exerted by a fluid on a surface is called THRUST. Pressure is the thrust acting per unit area, measured normal (perpendicular) to the surface:

   P = F / A

The SI unit of pressure is the pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m^2. Other units are the atmosphere (1 atm = 1.013 x 10^5 Pa), the bar (1 bar = 10^5 Pa) and mm of mercury (torr). Pressure is a SCALAR quantity - at a point in a fluid it acts equally in all directions.

7.2 PRESSURE AT A DEPTH IN A LIQUID

Consider a liquid of density rho at rest. Imagine a horizontal area A at depth h below the free surface. The column of liquid above it has volume A*h, mass rho*A*h and weight rho*A*h*g. This weight presses down on the area, so the pressure due to the liquid column is:

   P(due to liquid) = (rho * A * h * g) / A = h * rho * g

If the free surface is exposed to atmospheric pressure P0, the TOTAL (absolute) pressure at depth h is:

   P = P0 + h * rho * g

The pressure depends only on the depth h, the density rho and g - not on the shape or cross-section of the container. This is why pressure is the same at all points on a horizontal level in a connected liquid at rest (the basis of the hydrostatic paradox and of communicating vessels). The extra pressure h*rho*g is called the GAUGE PRESSURE.

Worked example: Find the pressure 10 m below the surface of a lake (rho = 1000 kg/m^3, g = 9.8 m/s^2, P0 = 1.0 x 10^5 Pa).
   Gauge pressure = h*rho*g = 10 x 1000 x 9.8 = 9.8 x 10^4 Pa.
   Absolute pressure = 1.0 x 10^5 + 9.8 x 10^4 = 1.98 x 10^5 Pa (about 2 atm).

7.3 PASCAL'S LAW AND HYDRAULIC MACHINES

PASCAL'S LAW states: the pressure applied to an enclosed fluid at rest is transmitted equally and undiminished to every part of the fluid and to the walls of the container.

This principle underlies HYDRAULIC MACHINES. In a hydraulic lift, a small force f is applied on a small piston of area a; this creates a pressure P = f/a which is transmitted to a large piston of area A. The upward force on the large piston is:

   F = P * A = f * (A / a)

Since A > a, the output force F is much greater than the input force f - the machine multiplies force by the factor A/a (mechanical advantage). Work is conserved: the small piston moves a large distance while the large piston moves a small distance. Hydraulic brakes, hydraulic presses and jacks all work on Pascal's law.

Worked example: A hydraulic lift has pistons of area a = 0.01 m^2 and A = 0.5 m^2. A force of 100 N is applied on the small piston. Find the load lifted.
   F = f*(A/a) = 100 x (0.5/0.01) = 100 x 50 = 5000 N.

7.4 ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURE

The atmosphere is a fluid (air) held to the Earth by gravity; its weight exerts a pressure on all objects. At sea level this ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURE is about 1.013 x 10^5 Pa. It was first measured by Torricelli using a mercury barometer: atmospheric pressure supports a column of mercury about 76 cm high. Using P = h*rho*g with h = 0.76 m and rho(Hg) = 13600 kg/m^3 gives P = 0.76 x 13600 x 9.8 = 1.013 x 10^5 Pa. Atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude, which is why aircraft cabins are pressurised and why cooking takes longer on high mountains.

7.5 BUOYANCY AND ARCHIMEDES' PRINCIPLE

When a body is immersed in a fluid, the fluid exerts an upward force on it called the BUOYANT FORCE (or upthrust). It arises because the pressure on the lower face of the body is greater than on the upper face (pressure increases with depth).

ARCHIMEDES' PRINCIPLE states: when a body is wholly or partly immersed in a fluid, it experiences an upthrust equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the body.

   Buoyant force = weight of displaced fluid = V * rho(fluid) * g

where V is the volume of fluid displaced (equal to the submerged volume of the body). The apparent weight of a submerged body = true weight - buoyant force.

LAW OF FLOATATION: A body floats when the buoyant force balances its weight. For a floating body, the weight of the body equals the weight of the fluid displaced. The fraction submerged equals the ratio of the body's density to the fluid's density: (V_submerged / V_body) = rho(body) / rho(fluid). This is why about 90 percent of an iceberg lies below the water surface (ice density about 917 kg/m^3, sea water about 1025 kg/m^3).

Worked example: A block of wood of density 600 kg/m^3 floats in water. What fraction is submerged?
   fraction = rho(body)/rho(fluid) = 600/1000 = 0.6, so 60 percent is submerged.

7.6 SURFACE TENSION

The free surface of a liquid behaves like a stretched elastic membrane. This property is SURFACE TENSION. Molecular basis: molecules of a liquid attract each other by COHESIVE forces. A molecule deep inside the liquid is pulled equally in all directions, so the net force on it is zero. A molecule at the surface has no liquid molecules above it, so it experiences a net INWARD pull. This makes the surface behave as if under tension and tends to minimise the surface area - which is why small drops are spherical (a sphere has the least surface area for a given volume).

Surface tension T is defined as the force per unit length acting along a line drawn on the liquid surface, perpendicular to it: T = F / L. Its SI unit is N/m. Equivalently, SURFACE ENERGY is the work done in increasing the surface area by unit amount; numerically T (in N/m) equals the surface energy per unit area (in J/m^2).

ADHESION is the attraction between molecules of different substances (e.g. water and glass). The balance of cohesion and adhesion decides the ANGLE OF CONTACT (theta) - the angle between the tangent to the liquid surface and the solid surface, measured inside the liquid. For water on clean glass, adhesion dominates, theta is small (nearly 0 degrees) and the liquid wets the surface (concave meniscus). For mercury on glass, cohesion dominates, theta is obtuse (about 140 degrees) and the liquid does not wet the surface (convex meniscus).

7.7 CAPILLARITY AND EXCESS PRESSURE

CAPILLARITY (capillary action) is the rise or fall of a liquid in a narrow tube (capillary) held vertically in the liquid. If the liquid wets the tube (theta acute), it RISES; if it does not wet (theta obtuse, like mercury), it is DEPRESSED. The height of capillary rise is:

   h = (2 * T * cos(theta)) / (r * rho * g)

where r is the tube radius, rho the liquid density and g the acceleration due to gravity. Note h is inversely proportional to r - narrower tubes give greater rise. Capillarity explains the rise of oil in a wick, water moving up through soil and the roots/stems of plants, and the action of blotting paper and towels.

EXCESS PRESSURE inside a curved surface: because of surface tension, the pressure inside a curved liquid surface is greater than outside. For a spherical LIQUID DROP (one surface):

   excess pressure = 2T / r

For a SOAP BUBBLE (two surfaces, inner and outer):

   excess pressure = 4T / r

Smaller drops/bubbles have larger excess pressure - which is why, when two bubbles of different size are connected, air flows from the smaller (higher pressure) into the larger one.

Worked example (capillary rise): Water (T = 0.072 N/m, rho = 1000 kg/m^3) rises in a capillary of radius 0.2 mm with theta = 0. Find h.
   h = 2T cos(theta)/(r rho g) = (2 x 0.072 x 1)/(0.0002 x 1000 x 9.8) = 0.144 / 1.96 = 0.0735 m = 7.35 cm.

7.8 VISCOSITY

When one layer of a fluid moves over another, there is internal friction opposing the relative motion. This property is VISCOSITY. Consider a fluid flowing in layers (laminar flow) with a velocity that varies from layer to layer. The velocity gradient dv/dx is the rate at which velocity changes with distance perpendicular to the flow. According to NEWTON'S LAW OF VISCOUS FORCE, the viscous drag F between two layers of area A is:

   F = eta * A * (dv/dx)

where eta (Greek letter, "eta") is the COEFFICIENT OF VISCOSITY of the fluid. Its SI unit is the pascal-second (Pa s) or N s/m^2; the CGS unit is the poise (1 Pa s = 10 poise). Liquids are more viscous than gases; the viscosity of a liquid decreases as temperature rises (its molecules move more freely), while for a gas it increases with temperature.

STOKES' LAW: A small sphere of radius r moving with velocity v through a fluid of viscosity eta experiences a viscous (retarding) force:

   F = 6 * pi * eta * r * v

TERMINAL VELOCITY: When a small sphere (e.g. a rain drop or a ball) falls through a viscous fluid, it accelerates at first; but the viscous drag increases with speed. Eventually the net force becomes zero - the weight is balanced by the buoyant force plus the viscous drag - and the body falls with a constant TERMINAL VELOCITY v_t. Setting the forces equal:

   (4/3) pi r^3 (rho - sigma) g = 6 pi eta r v_t

so   v_t = (2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g) / (9 eta)

where rho is the density of the sphere and sigma the density of the fluid. Terminal velocity is proportional to r^2 - larger drops fall faster. This explains why fine mist droplets almost float while large rain drops fall quickly, and it is the basis of Millikan's oil-drop experiment.

Worked example (terminal velocity): A steel ball of radius 1 mm (rho = 8000 kg/m^3) falls through oil (sigma = 900 kg/m^3, eta = 0.99 Pa s). Find v_t (g = 9.8).
   v_t = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g / (9 eta) = 2 x (0.001)^2 x (8000-900) x 9.8 / (9 x 0.99)
       = 2 x 1e-6 x 7100 x 9.8 / 8.91 = 0.1392 / 8.91 = 0.0156 m/s (about 1.6 cm/s).

7.9 FLUID FLOW: STREAMLINE AND TURBULENT

Fluid flow can be STREAMLINE (laminar) or TURBULENT. In streamline flow, every fluid particle passing a given point follows the same smooth path (streamline) with the same velocity; the layers slide over one another without mixing. In turbulent flow, the motion is irregular, with eddies and mixing. The nature of flow is decided by the REYNOLDS NUMBER:

   Re = (rho * v * D) / eta

where D is a characteristic dimension (e.g. pipe diameter). Flow is generally streamline for Re below about 2000 and turbulent above about 3000, with a transition region in between.

7.10 EQUATION OF CONTINUITY

For the steady flow of an incompressible fluid through a pipe of varying cross-section, mass is conserved. The mass entering per second must equal the mass leaving per second, so:

   A * v = constant, i.e. A1 v1 = A2 v2

This is the EQUATION OF CONTINUITY. It shows that where the pipe is narrow (small A) the fluid moves fast (large v), and where it is wide the fluid moves slowly. This is why water speeds up when you partly cover the mouth of a hose.

7.11 BERNOULLI'S THEOREM

For the steady, streamline flow of an ideal (non-viscous, incompressible) fluid, the total energy per unit volume is conserved along a streamline. BERNOULLI'S THEOREM states:

   P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant

Here P is the pressure energy per unit volume, (1/2) rho v^2 is the kinetic energy per unit volume and rho g h is the potential energy per unit volume. In words: where the speed of a fluid is high, the pressure is low, and vice versa.

Applications of Bernoulli's theorem:
 - VENTURIMETER: a tube with a constriction used to measure flow rate. The fluid speeds up in the narrow throat (continuity), so its pressure drops (Bernoulli). Measuring the pressure difference gives the speed and hence the volume flow rate.
 - AEROFOIL / LIFT: an aircraft wing is shaped so that air travels faster over the curved upper surface than the flatter lower surface. Faster flow means lower pressure on top, so the higher pressure below provides an upward LIFT.
 - ATOMISER / SPRAYER: squeezing a bulb blows air fast across the top of a tube dipped in liquid; the fast air has low pressure, so atmospheric pressure pushes the liquid up the tube, where it is broken into a spray.
 - The spin of a ball (Magnus effect) and the lift of a spinning cricket ball are also explained by Bernoulli's principle.

Worked example (Bernoulli/continuity): Water flows through a horizontal pipe that narrows from area 10 cm^2 to 5 cm^2. If the speed in the wide part is 2 m/s, find the speed in the narrow part.
   A1 v1 = A2 v2 => v2 = A1 v1 / A2 = (10 x 2)/5 = 4 m/s.

SUMMARY

- Pressure P = F/A (Pa = N/m^2); at depth h in a liquid, P = P0 + h rho g. Pressure acts equally in all directions and depends only on depth.
- Pascal's law: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished; hydraulic machines multiply force by A/a.
- Archimedes' principle: upthrust = weight of displaced fluid = V rho g. A body floats when its weight equals the weight of fluid displaced; fraction submerged = rho(body)/rho(fluid).
- Surface tension T = F/L (N/m) arises from cohesion; the surface minimises its area. Angle of contact theta depends on cohesion vs adhesion.
- Capillary rise h = 2T cos(theta)/(r rho g). Excess pressure inside a drop = 2T/r, inside a soap bubble = 4T/r.
- Viscosity: F = eta A (dv/dx); Stokes' law F = 6 pi eta r v; terminal velocity v_t = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g/(9 eta).
- Flow is streamline or turbulent (Reynolds number Re = rho v D/eta). Equation of continuity: A v = constant.
- Bernoulli's theorem: P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant; explains venturimeter, aerofoil lift and atomiser.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Properties of Fluids (NIOS Senior Secondary Physics)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Take g = 9.8 m/s^2 and density of water = 1000 kg/m^3 unless stated otherwise. Show all steps in numerical problems and derivations.

questions.question: Derive an expression for the pressure at a depth h below the free surface of a liquid of density rho, and hence write the total (absolute) pressure if the surface is exposed to atmospheric pressure P0.
questions.answer:
Consider a horizontal area A at depth h below the free surface of a liquid of density rho. The liquid column directly above this area has volume V = A*h, mass m = rho*A*h and weight W = m*g = rho*A*h*g. This weight acts vertically down on the area A.
Pressure due to the liquid column = force/area = (rho*A*h*g)/A = h*rho*g.
This result depends only on the depth h, the density rho and g - not on the shape or cross-section of the container.
If the free surface is exposed to the atmosphere at pressure P0, then by adding the atmospheric contribution the total (absolute) pressure at depth h is:
   P = P0 + h*rho*g.
The term h*rho*g is called the gauge pressure. This is why pressure is the same at all points on any horizontal level in a connected liquid at rest.
questions.explanation: Weight of the liquid column above unit area gives h rho g; add P0 for absolute pressure.

questions.question: State Pascal's law. In a hydraulic lift the small piston has area 0.02 m^2 and the large piston has area 0.8 m^2. If a force of 200 N is applied to the small piston, what maximum load can be lifted?
questions.answer:
Pascal's law: the pressure applied to an enclosed fluid at rest is transmitted equally and undiminished to every part of the fluid and to the walls of the container.
The applied pressure P = f/a = 200/0.02 = 10000 Pa is transmitted to the large piston.
Force on the large piston F = P*A = 10000 x 0.8 = 8000 N.
(Equivalently F = f*(A/a) = 200 x (0.8/0.02) = 200 x 40 = 8000 N.)
So the lift can raise a load of 8000 N - the machine multiplies the force by the area ratio 40.

questions.question: A block of density 750 kg/m^3 floats in water (1000 kg/m^3). (a) What fraction of its volume is submerged? (b) If the block has volume 0.02 m^3, find the volume above the water.
questions.answer:
(a) For a floating body the fraction submerged = rho(body)/rho(fluid) = 750/1000 = 0.75. So 75 percent of the volume is under water.
(b) Submerged volume = 0.75 x 0.02 = 0.015 m^3. Volume above the water = 0.02 - 0.015 = 0.005 m^3 (that is 25 percent, 0.005 m^3).
questions.explanation: Fraction submerged = density ratio = 0.75; above = 0.25 x 0.02 = 0.005 m^3.

questions.question: Explain the molecular origin of surface tension. Why do small liquid drops take a spherical shape?
questions.answer:
Molecules of a liquid attract each other through cohesive forces. A molecule deep inside the liquid is surrounded on all sides, so the cohesive forces cancel and the net force on it is zero. A molecule at the free surface has no liquid molecules above it, so it feels a net INWARD pull toward the bulk. As a result the surface behaves like a stretched elastic membrane under tension and tends to contract to the smallest possible area. This property is surface tension, T = F/L.
Because the surface tends to minimise its area, and a sphere has the least surface area for a given volume, small liquid drops (where surface tension dominates over gravity) take up a spherical shape.
questions.explanation: Unbalanced inward cohesive pull at the surface; sphere minimises surface area.

questions.question: Water of surface tension 0.072 N/m rises in a capillary tube of radius 0.25 mm. Taking the angle of contact as zero, calculate the height of the capillary rise (rho = 1000 kg/m^3, g = 9.8 m/s^2).
questions.answer:
Capillary rise formula: h = 2 T cos(theta) / (r rho g).
Given T = 0.072 N/m, theta = 0 so cos(theta) = 1, r = 0.25 mm = 0.00025 m, rho = 1000, g = 9.8.
h = (2 x 0.072 x 1) / (0.00025 x 1000 x 9.8)
  = 0.144 / 2.45
  = 0.0588 m
  = 5.88 cm (approximately).
So the water rises about 5.9 cm in the tube.

questions.question: A soap bubble and a liquid drop each have radius 2 mm. The surface tension of the soap solution is 0.03 N/m and that of the liquid is 0.072 N/m. Find the excess pressure inside each.
questions.answer:
For a spherical liquid drop (one surface): excess pressure = 2T/r.
Drop: r = 2 mm = 0.002 m, T = 0.072 N/m.
  excess pressure = 2 x 0.072 / 0.002 = 0.144/0.002 = 72 Pa.
For a soap bubble (two surfaces, inner and outer): excess pressure = 4T/r.
Bubble: r = 0.002 m, T = 0.03 N/m.
  excess pressure = 4 x 0.03 / 0.002 = 0.12/0.002 = 60 Pa.
So the excess pressure is 72 Pa inside the drop and 60 Pa inside the soap bubble.

questions.question: Derive the expression for the terminal velocity of a small sphere falling through a viscous fluid. Then find the terminal velocity of a steel ball of radius 0.5 mm and density 8000 kg/m^3 falling through glycerine (density 1260 kg/m^3, viscosity 0.83 Pa s).
questions.answer:
Derivation: A sphere of radius r and density rho falling through a fluid of density sigma and viscosity eta experiences three forces:
 - weight (down) = (4/3) pi r^3 rho g
 - buoyant force (up) = (4/3) pi r^3 sigma g
 - viscous drag (up, Stokes' law) = 6 pi eta r v.
At terminal velocity the net force is zero, so the downward weight equals the sum of the upward forces:
   (4/3) pi r^3 rho g = (4/3) pi r^3 sigma g + 6 pi eta r v_t.
Hence (4/3) pi r^3 (rho - sigma) g = 6 pi eta r v_t.
Solving for v_t:
   v_t = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g / (9 eta).
Numerical: r = 0.5 mm = 0.0005 m, rho = 8000, sigma = 1260, eta = 0.83, g = 9.8.
   v_t = 2 x (0.0005)^2 x (8000 - 1260) x 9.8 / (9 x 0.83)
       = 2 x 2.5e-7 x 6740 x 9.8 / 7.47
       = 0.03303 / 7.47
       = 0.00442 m/s (about 4.4 mm/s).

questions.question: Water flows through a horizontal pipe whose cross-sectional area falls from 8 cm^2 to 2 cm^2. If the speed in the wide section is 1.5 m/s, find the speed in the narrow section.
questions.answer:
By the equation of continuity for an incompressible fluid, A1 v1 = A2 v2.
So v2 = A1 v1 / A2 = (8 x 1.5) / 2 = 12 / 2 = 6 m/s.
The water moves four times faster where the pipe is one-quarter as wide.

questions.question: State Bernoulli's theorem and explain, using it, how an aeroplane wing (aerofoil) generates lift and how an atomiser works.
questions.answer:
Bernoulli's theorem: for the steady streamline flow of an ideal (non-viscous, incompressible) fluid, the sum of the pressure energy, kinetic energy and potential energy per unit volume is constant along a streamline:
   P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant.
A key consequence is that where the fluid speed is high, the pressure is low, and vice versa.
Aerofoil lift: an aircraft wing is shaped so its upper surface is more curved than its lower surface. Air travels a longer path and moves FASTER over the top than underneath. By Bernoulli's theorem the faster flow over the top has LOWER pressure than the slower flow below. The higher pressure below the wing therefore pushes it up, giving an upward LIFT.
Atomiser: squeezing the bulb blows air rapidly across the top of a vertical tube dipped in liquid. The fast-moving air has low pressure, so the higher atmospheric pressure on the liquid surface in the container pushes the liquid up the tube. At the top the emerging liquid meets the fast air stream and is broken up into a fine spray.
questions.explanation: P + 1/2 rho v^2 + rho g h = const; faster flow = lower pressure -> lift and atomiser suction.

questions.question: Distinguish between streamline and turbulent flow, and state how the Reynolds number decides which occurs.
questions.answer:
In STREAMLINE (laminar) flow every fluid particle passing a given point follows the same smooth path with the same velocity; the layers slide over one another without mixing. In TURBULENT flow the motion is irregular, with eddies and mixing, and the velocity at a point changes erratically.
The type of flow is decided by the Reynolds number Re = rho v D / eta (D = characteristic size, e.g. pipe diameter). Flow is generally streamline for small Re (below about 2000) and turbulent for large Re (above about 3000), with a transition region in between.
questions.explanation: Laminar = ordered layers; turbulent = eddies. Re = rho v D/eta; low Re laminar, high Re turbulent.

questions.question: Define pressure and state its SI unit.
questions.answer: Pressure is the thrust (normal force) acting per unit area on a surface: P = F/A. Its SI unit is the pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m^2. Pressure is a scalar quantity and, at a point in a fluid at rest, acts equally in all directions.

questions.question: Calculate the total pressure at the bottom of a tank of water 4 m deep. Take P0 = 1.0 x 10^5 Pa, rho = 1000, g = 9.8.
questions.answer:
Gauge (column) pressure = h rho g = 4 x 1000 x 9.8 = 39200 Pa = 3.92 x 10^4 Pa.
Total (absolute) pressure = P0 + h rho g = 1.0 x 10^5 + 3.92 x 10^4 = 1.392 x 10^5 Pa.
So the pressure at the bottom is about 1.39 x 10^5 Pa.

questions.question: State and briefly explain the hydrostatic paradox.
questions.answer: The hydrostatic paradox says that the pressure at the bottom of a liquid depends only on the vertical depth, the density and g - NOT on the shape or amount of liquid or the cross-section of the vessel. So three vessels of very different shapes but the same liquid depth have the same pressure at the base, even though they contain different amounts of liquid. This follows from P = P0 + h rho g, which contains no term for shape or volume.
questions.explanation: Pressure depends only on depth; shape/volume irrelevant.

questions.question: In a hydraulic press the areas of the two pistons are 5 cm^2 and 200 cm^2. A force of 25 N is applied on the smaller piston. Find the force on the larger piston and the mechanical advantage.
questions.answer:
Pressure applied = f/a = 25/(5 x 10^-4) = 50000 Pa.
Force on larger piston F = P x A = 50000 x (200 x 10^-4) = 50000 x 0.02 = 1000 N.
(Or F = f (A/a) = 25 x (200/5) = 25 x 40 = 1000 N.)
Mechanical advantage = A/a = 200/5 = 40. So the press multiplies the force 40 times.

questions.question: Why is a hydraulic brake system able to apply equal braking force at all four wheels?
questions.answer: A hydraulic brake uses Pascal's law: when the brake pedal presses the master-cylinder piston, the pressure produced in the brake fluid is transmitted equally and undiminished through the connecting pipes to the wheel cylinders at all four wheels. Because the pressure is the same everywhere, each wheel cylinder of equal area exerts the same force on its brake, giving balanced braking.
questions.explanation: Pascal's law transmits equal pressure to all wheel cylinders.

questions.question: State Archimedes' principle and define apparent weight.
questions.answer:
Archimedes' principle: a body wholly or partly immersed in a fluid experiences an upthrust (buoyant force) equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces, i.e. upthrust = V rho(fluid) g.
Apparent weight is the weight of the body as measured while it is immersed; it equals the true weight minus the upthrust: W(apparent) = W(true) - upthrust.
questions.explanation: Upthrust = weight of displaced fluid; apparent weight = true weight - upthrust.

questions.question: A metal cube weighs 60 N in air and 52 N when fully immersed in water. Find (a) the upthrust, (b) the volume of the cube, (c) its density. (rho water = 1000, g = 9.8)
questions.answer:
(a) Upthrust = loss of weight in water = 60 - 52 = 8 N.
(b) Upthrust = V rho(water) g, so V = 8/(1000 x 9.8) = 8/9800 = 8.16 x 10^-4 m^3.
(c) Mass of cube = W/g = 60/9.8 = 6.12 kg. Density = mass/volume = 6.12/8.16e-4 = 7500 kg/m^3 (approximately).
questions.explanation: Upthrust 8 N; V = 8.16e-4 m^3; density about 7500 kg/m^3.

questions.question: Explain why a ship made of steel floats although a solid lump of the same steel sinks.
questions.answer: Whether a body floats depends on its AVERAGE density compared with water, not on the material alone. A solid steel lump has density much greater than water, so it sinks. A ship is hollow: its large volume encloses a lot of air, so the average density of the whole ship (steel + enclosed space) is less than that of water. It therefore displaces a weight of water equal to its own weight while only partly submerged, and floats.
questions.explanation: Ship's average density (with hollow) is less than water; the lump's is greater.

questions.question: Distinguish between cohesion and adhesion, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: COHESION is the force of attraction between molecules of the SAME substance - for example, the attraction between water molecules that holds a drop together and gives rise to surface tension. ADHESION is the force of attraction between molecules of DIFFERENT substances - for example, the attraction between water and glass that makes water wet (spread on) a glass surface.
questions.explanation: Cohesion: like molecules (water-water). Adhesion: unlike molecules (water-glass).

questions.question: Explain, in terms of the angle of contact, why water wets glass but mercury does not.
questions.answer:
The angle of contact theta is measured inside the liquid between the tangent to its surface and the solid.
For water on clean glass, the adhesion between water and glass is stronger than the cohesion among water molecules. The water spreads on the glass, the meniscus is concave, and theta is small (close to 0 degrees) - the liquid WETS the surface.
For mercury on glass, the cohesion among mercury atoms is much stronger than its adhesion to glass. The mercury pulls itself into rounded drops, the meniscus is convex, and theta is obtuse (about 140 degrees) - the liquid does NOT wet the surface.
questions.explanation: Wetting: adhesion > cohesion, theta acute. Non-wetting: cohesion > adhesion, theta obtuse.

questions.question: What is meant by surface energy, and how is it related to surface tension?
questions.answer: Surface energy is the extra potential energy possessed by the molecules at the surface of a liquid compared with those in the bulk; equivalently, it is the work that must be done to increase the surface area by unit amount. It is measured in J/m^2. Numerically the surface tension T (in N/m) is equal to the surface energy per unit area (in J/m^2), because increasing the area by dA against a surface tension T requires work T dA.
questions.explanation: Surface energy = work to create unit area; numerically equals T.

questions.question: A capillary tube of radius 0.4 mm is dipped in water (T = 0.072 N/m, theta = 0). Find the capillary rise and the mass of water in the raised column if the tube radius is 0.4 mm. (rho = 1000, g = 9.8)
Calculate the excess pressure inside an air bubble of radius 1 mm formed inside water (T = 0.072 N/m).
questions.answer:
An air bubble inside water has a single liquid surface, so the excess pressure is 2T/r (like a drop).
Excess pressure = 2T/r = (2 x 0.072)/(0.001) = 0.144/0.001 = 144 Pa.
So the pressure inside the bubble exceeds that of the surrounding water by 144 Pa.
questions.explanation: Air bubble in water has one surface: 2T/r = 144 Pa.

questions.question: Give two everyday examples of capillary action and explain them briefly.
questions.answer:
(1) Rise of oil in the wick of a lamp: the narrow spaces between the fibres of the wick act as fine capillaries, and oil rises through them by capillarity to feed the flame.
(2) Absorption of water by a towel or blotting paper: the tiny pores act as capillaries, drawing water up and into the material. (Other examples: water rising in soil to reach plant roots, ink spreading on paper.)
questions.explanation: Wick of a lamp and blotting paper/towel - narrow pores act as capillaries.

questions.question: State Newton's law of viscous force and name the quantity eta.
questions.answer:
Newton's law of viscous force: the tangential viscous force F between two layers of a fluid in laminar flow is proportional to the area of contact A and to the velocity gradient dv/dx perpendicular to the flow:
   F = eta A (dv/dx).
Here eta is the coefficient of viscosity of the fluid, a measure of its internal friction; its SI unit is the pascal-second (Pa s).
questions.explanation: F = eta A (dv/dx); eta = coefficient of viscosity (Pa s).

questions.question: A raindrop of radius 0.2 mm falls through air (eta = 1.8 x 10^-5 Pa s). Taking the density of the drop as 1000 kg/m^3 and neglecting air density, find its terminal velocity. (g = 9.8)
questions.answer:
Neglecting the density of air (sigma is negligible compared with rho = 1000):
   v_t = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g/(9 eta) = 2 x (0.0002)^2 x 1000 x 9.8/(9 x 1.8e-5).
Numerator = 2 x 4e-8 x 1000 x 9.8 = 2 x 4e-8 x 9800 = 7.84e-4.
Denominator = 9 x 1.8e-5 = 1.62e-4.
v_t = 7.84e-4/1.62e-4 = 4.84 m/s (approximately 4.8 m/s).

questions.question: Why does a raindrop reach a constant (terminal) speed instead of accelerating all the way down?
questions.answer: As the drop falls, its speed increases, and the viscous drag (Stokes' force, F = 6 pi eta r v) increases with speed. At first the weight exceeds the opposing forces and the drop accelerates. But the drag grows until the upward forces (buoyancy + viscous drag) exactly balance the downward weight. Then the net force is zero, the acceleration is zero, and the drop continues at a constant terminal velocity.
questions.explanation: Drag rises with speed until it balances weight; net force zero -> constant speed.

questions.question: State the equation of continuity and what physical quantity it expresses.
questions.answer: The equation of continuity for the steady flow of an incompressible fluid is A v = constant, i.e. A1 v1 = A2 v2, where A is the cross-sectional area of the pipe and v the fluid speed there. It expresses the conservation of MASS: the mass of fluid entering any section per second equals the mass leaving per second, so the fluid speeds up where the pipe narrows and slows where it widens.
questions.explanation: A v = constant; expresses conservation of mass.

questions.question: Water enters a pipe of diameter 4 cm at 2 m/s. What is its speed where the diameter narrows to 2 cm?
questions.answer:
Area is proportional to (diameter)^2. When the diameter halves (4 cm to 2 cm), the area becomes one quarter.
By continuity A1 v1 = A2 v2, so v2 = v1 (A1/A2) = 2 x 4 = 8 m/s.
(Check: A1/A2 = (4/2)^2 = 4.) The water speeds up to 8 m/s in the narrow section.
questions.explanation: Area drops to 1/4, so v2 = 4 x 2 = 8 m/s.

questions.question: What is the Reynolds number? Water (rho = 1000, eta = 1.0 x 10^-3 Pa s) flows at 0.5 m/s through a pipe of diameter 2 cm. Find the Reynolds number and state the type of flow.
questions.answer:
The Reynolds number Re = rho v D/eta is a dimensionless quantity (the ratio of inertial to viscous forces) that decides whether flow is streamline or turbulent.
Here Re = (1000 x 0.5 x 0.02)/(1.0e-3) = 10/1.0e-3 = 10000.
Since Re = 10000 is well above about 3000, the flow is TURBULENT.
questions.explanation: Re = rho v D/eta = 10000 (> 3000) -> turbulent flow.

questions.question: State Bernoulli's theorem and name the three energy terms in its equation.
questions.answer:
Bernoulli's theorem: for the steady, streamline flow of an ideal (non-viscous, incompressible) fluid, the total energy per unit volume is constant along a streamline:
   P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant.
The three terms are: P = pressure energy per unit volume; (1/2) rho v^2 = kinetic energy per unit volume; and rho g h = potential (gravitational) energy per unit volume. It is essentially a statement of the conservation of energy for a flowing fluid.
questions.explanation: P (pressure energy) + 1/2 rho v^2 (KE) + rho g h (PE) per unit volume = constant.

questions.question: Water flows steadily through a horizontal pipe. At a wide point the pressure is 2.0 x 10^5 Pa and speed 3 m/s; at a narrow point the speed is 5 m/s. Find the pressure there. (rho = 1000)
questions.answer:
For a horizontal pipe (h constant), Bernoulli gives P1 + (1/2) rho v1^2 = P2 + (1/2) rho v2^2.
P2 = P1 + (1/2) rho (v1^2 - v2^2) = 2.0e5 + 0.5 x 1000 x (9 - 25)
   = 2.0e5 + 500 x (-16) = 2.0e5 - 8000 = 1.92 x 10^5 Pa.
The pressure falls to 1.92 x 10^5 Pa where the water moves faster.

questions.question: Derive the expression P = P0 + h rho g for the pressure at a depth h in a liquid, and explain the term gauge pressure.
questions.answer:
Take a horizontal area A at depth h below the free surface of a liquid of density rho. The column of liquid directly above the area has volume A h, mass rho A h and weight rho A h g, which presses down on the area.
Pressure due to this liquid column = weight/area = (rho A h g)/A = h rho g.
If the free surface is exposed to the atmosphere at pressure P0, this atmospheric pressure is also transmitted down through the liquid (Pascal's law). Therefore the total (absolute) pressure at depth h is:
   P = P0 + h rho g.
The extra pressure h rho g, over and above the atmospheric pressure, is called the GAUGE PRESSURE - it is what an ordinary pressure gauge (which reads zero at atmospheric pressure) measures. The result depends only on depth, density and g, not on the shape of the vessel.
questions.explanation: Weight of column/area = h rho g; add P0. Gauge pressure = h rho g.

questions.question: Describe the principle and working of a hydraulic lift with a labelled explanation, and show how it multiplies force.
questions.answer:
A hydraulic lift consists of two cylinders of different cross-sectional areas connected at the bottom and filled with an incompressible liquid (oil). A small piston of area a is fitted in the narrow cylinder and a large piston of area A in the wide one.
Working: A force f is applied downward on the small piston. This creates a pressure P = f/a in the liquid. By PASCAL'S LAW this pressure is transmitted equally and undiminished through the liquid to the large piston. The upward force on the large piston is:
   F = P A = (f/a) A = f (A/a).
Since A > a, F is much larger than f - the lift multiplies force by the factor A/a (its mechanical advantage). This lets a small effort raise a heavy load such as a car.
Energy is conserved: to raise the large piston by a small distance, the small piston must be pushed through a much larger distance, so the work done by the effort equals the work done on the load (ignoring friction).
questions.explanation: P = f/a transmitted to area A -> F = f(A/a); work conserved.

questions.question: State the law of floatation. A wooden block of dimensions 0.5 m x 0.3 m x 0.2 m and density 600 kg/m^3 floats in water. Find (a) the weight of the block, (b) the volume submerged, (c) the depth to which it sinks (with the 0.2 m side vertical). (rho water = 1000, g = 9.8)
questions.answer:
Law of floatation: a body floats when the buoyant force (upthrust) equals its weight; equivalently, a floating body displaces a weight of fluid equal to its own weight.
Volume of block V = 0.5 x 0.3 x 0.2 = 0.03 m^3.
(a) Mass = rho V = 600 x 0.03 = 18 kg. Weight = m g = 18 x 9.8 = 176.4 N.
(b) For floating, weight of block = weight of water displaced = V(sub) rho(water) g.
   V(sub) = mass/rho(water) = 18/1000 = 0.018 m^3.
(Check: fraction submerged = 600/1000 = 0.6, and 0.6 x 0.03 = 0.018 m^3.)
(c) The horizontal cross-sectional area (base) = 0.5 x 0.3 = 0.15 m^2. Depth submerged d = V(sub)/area = 0.018/0.15 = 0.12 m.
So the block sinks to a depth of 0.12 m (that is, 60 percent of its 0.2 m height).
questions.explanation: Weight 176.4 N; V(sub) = 0.018 m^3; depth = 0.12 m (60 percent).

questions.question: Explain the molecular theory of surface tension and use it to account for (a) the spherical shape of small drops and (b) the ability of a small steel needle to float on water.
questions.answer:
Molecular theory: liquid molecules attract one another through cohesive forces, each effective over a small range. A molecule well inside the liquid is pulled equally in all directions, so the net cohesive force on it is zero. A molecule at or near the free surface has fewer liquid molecules above it, so it feels a NET INWARD pull. To bring a molecule from the interior to the surface, work must be done against this inward pull; hence surface molecules have extra energy and the surface behaves like a stretched membrane in a state of tension. This tendency to minimise surface area is surface tension, T = F/L.
(a) Spherical drops: for a given volume, a sphere has the least surface area. Since surface tension tends to make the surface area as small as possible, a small drop (where surface tension dominates over gravity) pulls itself into a sphere.
(b) Floating needle: a small, dry (or greased) steel needle placed gently on water depresses the surface, which behaves like a stretched membrane. The surface tension acting along the contact line has an upward component that, together with buoyancy, can balance the small weight of the needle, so it floats even though steel is denser than water. (If the surface is broken or a detergent lowers T, the needle sinks.)
questions.explanation: Unbalanced inward pull at surface -> tension; sphere minimises area; surface film supports the needle.

questions.question: Derive the formula for the height of capillary rise, h = 2T cos(theta)/(r rho g), and use it to find the surface tension of a liquid that rises 4 cm in a tube of radius 0.3 mm (rho = 800 kg/m^3, theta = 0, g = 9.8).
questions.answer:
Derivation: Consider a capillary tube of radius r held vertically in a wetting liquid of surface tension T and density rho. The liquid rises to height h. The surface tension acts along the circle of contact (length 2 pi r) at angle theta to the tube wall. The upward vertical component of this force is:
   F(up) = T cos(theta) x (2 pi r).
This supports the weight of the raised liquid column (approximately a cylinder of height h):
   W = (pi r^2 h) rho g.
At equilibrium F(up) = W:
   T cos(theta) (2 pi r) = pi r^2 h rho g.
Cancelling pi r:
   2 T cos(theta) = r h rho g,
so   h = 2 T cos(theta)/(r rho g).
Numerical: rearrange for T: T = h r rho g/(2 cos(theta)).
With h = 0.04 m, r = 0.0003 m, rho = 800, g = 9.8, cos(theta) = 1:
   T = (0.04 x 0.0003 x 800 x 9.8)/(2 x 1) = (0.09408)/2 = 0.047 N/m.
So the surface tension is about 0.047 N/m.
questions.explanation: Balance 2 pi r T cos(theta) = pi r^2 h rho g -> h = 2T cos(theta)/(r rho g); T = 0.047 N/m.

questions.question: Using Stokes' law, derive the expression for the terminal velocity of a sphere falling through a viscous fluid, and explain how this idea is used in Millikan's oil-drop experiment.
questions.answer:
Consider a sphere of radius r and density rho falling through a fluid of density sigma and viscosity eta. Three forces act on it:
 - weight downward: W = (4/3) pi r^3 rho g
 - buoyant force upward: U = (4/3) pi r^3 sigma g
 - viscous drag upward (Stokes' law): F = 6 pi eta r v.
As the sphere speeds up, the drag increases until the net force becomes zero; the sphere then moves at constant terminal velocity v_t. At that stage:
   W = U + F
   (4/3) pi r^3 rho g = (4/3) pi r^3 sigma g + 6 pi eta r v_t.
So (4/3) pi r^3 (rho - sigma) g = 6 pi eta r v_t, giving:
   v_t = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g/(9 eta).
Millikan's oil-drop experiment: tiny charged oil drops are sprayed between two horizontal plates. With no field, a drop falls at its terminal velocity, and measuring v_t (with the equation above) gives the drop's radius, hence its mass. An electric field is then applied to hold a charged drop stationary or move it, letting Millikan calculate the charge on the drop. He found the charge was always an integer multiple of a basic value - the charge of the electron, e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C.
questions.explanation: Balance weight = buoyancy + Stokes drag -> v_t = 2 r^2 (rho-sigma) g/(9 eta); used to size drops in Millikan's experiment.

questions.question: Explain the working of a venturimeter using Bernoulli's theorem and the equation of continuity.
questions.answer:
A venturimeter is a horizontal tube with a wide section that narrows to a throat and then widens again; it measures the rate of flow of a liquid. Pressure gauges (or vertical tubes) are fitted at the wide section (area A1) and the throat (area A2).
By the equation of continuity, A1 v1 = A2 v2. Since A2 < A1, the liquid moves FASTER in the throat (v2 > v1).
By Bernoulli's theorem for the horizontal tube, P1 + (1/2) rho v1^2 = P2 + (1/2) rho v2^2. Because v2 > v1, the pressure P2 in the throat is LESS than P1 in the wide section. This pressure difference (P1 - P2) shows up as a difference in liquid levels in the two vertical tubes.
Measuring (P1 - P2) and knowing A1 and A2, one uses these two equations together to calculate the flow speed and hence the volume of liquid flowing per second (the flow rate). Thus the venturimeter turns an easily measured pressure difference into a measurement of flow rate.
questions.explanation: Continuity: throat is faster; Bernoulli: faster -> lower pressure; measured pressure drop gives flow rate.

questions.question: Water flows through a pipe that rises from a lower wide section (area 20 cm^2, speed 1 m/s, pressure 1.5 x 10^5 Pa, at height 0) to an upper narrow section (area 5 cm^2, height 2 m). Using continuity and Bernoulli's theorem, find the speed and pressure in the upper section. (rho = 1000, g = 9.8)
questions.answer:
Step 1 - continuity: A1 v1 = A2 v2, so v2 = A1 v1/A2 = (20 x 1)/5 = 4 m/s.
Step 2 - Bernoulli between the two sections:
   P1 + (1/2) rho v1^2 + rho g h1 = P2 + (1/2) rho v2^2 + rho g h2.
With h1 = 0, h2 = 2 m:
   P2 = P1 + (1/2) rho (v1^2 - v2^2) + rho g (h1 - h2)
      = 1.5e5 + 0.5 x 1000 x (1 - 16) + 1000 x 9.8 x (0 - 2)
      = 1.5e5 + 500 x (-15) + (-19600)
      = 1.5e5 - 7500 - 19600
      = 1.5e5 - 27100
      = 1.229 x 10^5 Pa.
So in the upper section the water flows at 4 m/s and the pressure is about 1.23 x 10^5 Pa (it falls because the water is both faster and higher).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A dam holds back water in a reservoir. Engineers know that the pressure exerted by the water on the dam wall increases with depth, so dams are built much thicker at the base than at the top. A diver also feels increasing pressure on the ears as she descends.

(i) Write the formula for the gauge pressure at depth h.
(ii) Why is a dam made thicker at its base?
(iii) Find the gauge pressure at a depth of 30 m of water (rho = 1000, g = 9.8).
(iv) Does this pressure depend on the surface area of the reservoir?
questions.answer:
(i) Gauge pressure at depth h = h rho g.
(ii) Because pressure increases with depth (h rho g), the water pushes hardest at the bottom of the wall. The base must be thicker to withstand this larger force without breaking.
(iii) Gauge pressure = h rho g = 30 x 1000 x 9.8 = 2.94 x 10^5 Pa.
(iv) No. The pressure depends only on the depth, the density and g - not on the surface area or total volume of the reservoir (hydrostatic paradox).
questions.explanation: P = h rho g increases with depth; at 30 m it is 2.94e5 Pa; independent of area.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A garage uses a hydraulic lift to raise cars. The small piston has area 4 x 10^-4 m^2 and the large piston has area 0.1 m^2. A pump applies a force of 80 N on the small piston.

(i) On what principle does the lift work?
(ii) What pressure is produced in the liquid?
(iii) What is the maximum load the lift can raise?
(iv) If the small piston moves down 0.5 m, how far does the large piston rise (ignoring losses)?
questions.answer:
(i) Pascal's law - pressure applied to the enclosed liquid is transmitted equally and undiminished.
(ii) Pressure P = f/a = 80/(4e-4) = 2.0 x 10^5 Pa.
(iii) Force on large piston F = P A = 2.0e5 x 0.1 = 2.0 x 10^4 N = 20000 N. (Or F = f (A/a) = 80 x (0.1/4e-4) = 80 x 250 = 20000 N.)
(iv) Work is conserved, and the liquid is incompressible so the volume pushed equals the volume raised: a x d(small) = A x d(large). d(large) = a d(small)/A = (4e-4 x 0.5)/0.1 = 2e-4/0.1 = 2 x 10^-3 m = 2 mm.
questions.explanation: Pascal's law; P = 2e5 Pa; F = 20000 N; large piston rises 2 mm.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A crown of mass 2 kg is suspended from a spring balance. In air it reads 19.6 N. When fully immersed in water the balance reads 17.6 N.

(i) What is the buoyant force on the crown?
(ii) What volume of water does the crown displace? (rho = 1000, g = 9.8)
(iii) What is the volume of the crown?
(iv) Find the density of the crown and comment on whether it could be pure gold (density 19300 kg/m^3).
questions.answer:
(i) Buoyant force = apparent loss of weight = 19.6 - 17.6 = 2.0 N.
(ii) Buoyant force = V rho(water) g, so V = 2.0/(1000 x 9.8) = 2.04 x 10^-4 m^3 of water displaced.
(iii) The crown is fully immersed, so its volume equals the volume of water displaced: V(crown) = 2.04 x 10^-4 m^3.
(iv) Density = mass/volume = 2/2.04e-4 = 9800 kg/m^3 (approximately). This is far less than 19300 kg/m^3, so the crown is NOT pure gold - it must be an alloy or partly hollow. (This is the classic Archimedes problem.)
questions.explanation: Upthrust 2 N; V = 2.04e-4 m^3; density about 9800 kg/m^3 - not pure gold.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Water striders (pond skaters) walk on the surface of ponds without sinking. If a little detergent is added to the water, the insects can no longer stay afloat. Meanwhile, water forms a concave meniscus in a glass tube but mercury forms a convex one.

(i) Which property of the liquid surface supports the insect?
(ii) Why does adding detergent make the insect sink?
(iii) Explain the concave meniscus of water in terms of adhesion and cohesion.
(iv) Why is the mercury meniscus convex?
questions.answer:
(i) Surface tension - the free surface behaves like a stretched membrane that can support the insect's small weight.
(ii) Detergent is a surfactant that greatly REDUCES the surface tension of water. With a weaker surface film, the surface can no longer support the insect's weight, so it sinks.
(iii) For water in glass, ADHESION (water-glass) is stronger than COHESION (water-water). Water is pulled up along the glass wall, the edges rise, and the surface curves upward at the sides - a concave meniscus; the angle of contact is small.
(iv) For mercury in glass, COHESION (mercury-mercury) is much stronger than adhesion to glass. Mercury pulls itself together and away from the glass, so the surface bulges up in the middle - a convex meniscus; the angle of contact is obtuse.
questions.explanation: Surface tension supports the insect; detergent lowers T; adhesion>cohesion gives concave water meniscus, cohesion>adhesion gives convex mercury meniscus.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Sap rises in tall plants partly through very fine tubes (xylem), an example of capillarity. A student models this with a glass capillary of radius 0.1 mm dipped in water (T = 0.072 N/m, theta = 0, rho = 1000, g = 9.8).

(i) Write the capillary-rise formula.
(ii) Calculate the height to which water rises in this tube.
(iii) What happens to the rise if the radius is doubled to 0.2 mm?
(iv) Would mercury rise or fall in the same tube? Why?
questions.answer:
(i) h = 2 T cos(theta)/(r rho g).
(ii) h = (2 x 0.072 x 1)/(0.0001 x 1000 x 9.8) = 0.144/0.98 = 0.147 m = 14.7 cm.
(iii) Since h is inversely proportional to r, doubling r to 0.2 mm HALVES the rise: h = 14.7/2 = 7.35 cm.
(iv) Mercury would FALL (be depressed), not rise. Mercury does not wet glass; its angle of contact is obtuse (about 140 degrees), so cos(theta) is negative and h comes out negative, meaning a capillary depression.
questions.explanation: h = 0.144/0.98 = 0.147 m; doubling r halves h to 7.35 cm; mercury is depressed (obtuse theta).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Two soap bubbles of radii 3 cm and 1 cm (same soap solution, T = 0.025 N/m) are blown at the two ends of a tube and the tube between them is opened.

(i) Write the excess pressure inside a soap bubble.
(ii) Which bubble has the higher internal pressure?
(iii) Predict what happens when the connecting tube is opened.
(iv) Compute the excess pressure inside each bubble.
questions.answer:
(i) Excess pressure inside a soap bubble = 4T/r (two surfaces).
(ii) The SMALLER bubble (r = 1 cm) has the higher internal pressure, because excess pressure is inversely proportional to r.
(iii) When the tube is opened, air flows from the smaller (higher-pressure) bubble into the larger (lower-pressure) bubble. The small bubble shrinks and the large one grows.
(iv) Small bubble: 4T/r = 4 x 0.025/0.01 = 10 Pa. Large bubble: 4 x 0.025/0.03 = 3.33 Pa. The 10 Pa vs 3.33 Pa difference drives air from small to large.
questions.explanation: 4T/r; smaller bubble higher pressure (10 Pa vs 3.33 Pa); air flows small -> large.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A small glass sphere of radius 1 mm and density 2500 kg/m^3 is dropped into a tall jar of glycerine (density 1260 kg/m^3, viscosity 0.83 Pa s). It quickly reaches a steady speed.

(i) Name the steady speed and the three forces acting at that stage.
(ii) Write the formula for terminal velocity.
(iii) Calculate the terminal velocity. (g = 9.8)
(iv) What would happen to this speed if a larger sphere of the same glass were used?
questions.answer:
(i) The steady speed is the terminal velocity. The three forces are: weight (down), buoyant force (up), and viscous drag (up, given by Stokes' law).
(ii) v_t = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g/(9 eta).
(iii) r = 0.001 m, rho = 2500, sigma = 1260, eta = 0.83.
   v_t = 2 x (0.001)^2 x (2500 - 1260) x 9.8/(9 x 0.83)
       = 2 x 1e-6 x 1240 x 9.8/7.47
       = 0.0243/7.47 = 0.00325 m/s (about 3.3 mm/s).
(iv) A larger sphere would have a HIGHER terminal velocity, because v_t is proportional to r^2 - doubling the radius makes the terminal velocity four times as large.
questions.explanation: Terminal velocity; balance of weight, buoyancy, drag; v_t = 0.0243/7.47 = 0.0033 m/s; larger r -> larger v_t (r^2).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Water flows steadily through a horizontal pipe of circular cross-section. The pipe has a wide part of radius 2 cm and a narrow part of radius 1 cm. The water speed in the wide part is 1.2 m/s.

(i) State the equation of continuity.
(ii) Find the ratio of the cross-sectional areas.
(iii) Find the speed of the water in the narrow part.
(iv) In which part is the pressure greater, and why?
questions.answer:
(i) Equation of continuity: A1 v1 = A2 v2 (A v = constant) for an incompressible fluid.
(ii) Area is proportional to radius squared. A1/A2 = (2/1)^2 = 4. So the wide part has 4 times the area of the narrow part.
(iii) v2 = v1 (A1/A2) = 1.2 x 4 = 4.8 m/s.
(iv) The pressure is greater in the WIDE part. By Bernoulli's theorem, where the speed is lower (wide part) the pressure is higher, and where the speed is higher (narrow part) the pressure is lower.
questions.explanation: A v = constant; A1/A2 = 4; v2 = 4.8 m/s; pressure greater in the slower wide part.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

During a storm, the roof of a house is sometimes lifted off. Fast wind blows over the top of the roof while the air inside is comparatively still. A perfume atomiser works on the same underlying principle.

(i) Which principle explains both effects?
(ii) Why is the pressure above the roof lower than below it?
(iii) Explain how this lifts the roof.
(iv) Briefly explain how the atomiser sprays liquid.
questions.answer:
(i) Bernoulli's principle (P + 1/2 rho v^2 + rho g h = constant).
(ii) The wind moves fast over the roof, so by Bernoulli's theorem the pressure of the fast-moving air ABOVE the roof is lower than the pressure of the nearly still air inside/below the roof.
(iii) The higher pressure below the roof and lower pressure above create a net UPWARD force on the roof. If this exceeds the roof's weight and the strength of its fixings, the roof is lifted off.
(iv) In an atomiser, squeezing the bulb blows air rapidly across the top of a tube dipped in the liquid. The fast air has low pressure, so the higher atmospheric pressure on the liquid surface pushes the liquid up the tube; at the top it meets the air stream and breaks into a fine spray.
questions.explanation: Bernoulli: fast air above roof = low pressure -> net upward force; atomiser lifts liquid by the same low-pressure effect.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A large tank is filled with water to a height of 5 m above a small hole in its side. The tank is open to the atmosphere at the top. (Take g = 9.8, rho = 1000.)

(i) Apply Bernoulli's theorem between the top surface and the hole to derive the speed of efflux.
(ii) State the name of this result.
(iii) Calculate the speed of the water jet leaving the hole.
(iv) On what does this speed depend?
questions.answer:
(i) At the top surface and at the hole the pressure is atmospheric (P0), so those terms cancel. The top surface is (nearly) at rest and at height h above the hole. Bernoulli gives:
   P0 + 0 + rho g h = P0 + (1/2) rho v^2 + 0.
Hence (1/2) rho v^2 = rho g h, so v = sqrt(2 g h).
(ii) This is Torricelli's theorem (law of efflux).
(iii) v = sqrt(2 x 9.8 x 5) = sqrt(98) = 9.9 m/s (approximately).
(iv) The speed of efflux depends only on the height h of the liquid above the hole (and g) - the same as a body falling freely through height h. It does not depend on the density of the liquid.
questions.explanation: Bernoulli -> v = sqrt(2 g h) (Torricelli); v = sqrt(98) = 9.9 m/s; depends only on h.
